title: Writing my name
keyIdea: Your name is a set of letters that always go in the same order, so it says your name every time. To find your name card, check every letter, not just the first one: Lee and Leon start like Leo, but they are not Leo. Write your name from left to right. The first letter is a capital, a big letter, and the rest are small letters: Leo, not LEO or leo. Start each letter in the right place, such as o at the top. At first, copy it from your name card.
familyTip: Make a name card with your child's name written clearly: a capital first, then small letters, the way school will teach it. Stick it at their height and point to each letter as you say the name together. When they make marks or write, ask, 'What does that say?' and let them say, 'That says my name.' Praise every try, and let them copy from the card for as long as they need.

visual.caption: Is the first letter right? Drag each name, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: find your name card, build Leo with a big letter first, put letters in order, trace Leo and write your own name.

kid: Your name is made of letters. They go in the same order every time. That is how a name says your name.
To find your name card, look at every letter. Lee starts like Leo, but it ends in e. It is not Leo. Ole has Leo's letters, but they are mixed up. It is not Leo.
Write your name from left to right. The first letter is big. We call it a capital. The rest are small letters. Leo, not LEO, and not leo.
Start each letter at the right place. L starts at the top. o starts at the top and goes round. Look at your name card and copy it. Then say: that says my name!
adult: Ages 4 to 5. In the EYFS, Development Matters (2021) lists writing some or all of their name as a goal from age 3 to 4, and the Early Learning Goal for Writing at the end of Reception asks children to write recognisable letters, most of which are correctly formed. The DfE Writing framework (2025) treats a child's name as their first, most meaningful word to read and write: recognising it, then writing it from a model with correct letter formation.

Children often find their name card by its first letter alone, so Lee, Leon or Lea can pass as Leo. Checking every letter, in order, is the first step to reading words. Letter order is new too: young children may accept e L o as their name because all the letters are there.

Common mistakes: all capitals (LEO), all small letters (leo), a capital in the middle (LeO), writing from right to left, and starting letters at the bottom. Schools teach a capital first, then lower-case letters, because that is how names are written in books and on signs. Round letters such as o, a, c and d start at the top and go anticlockwise; e starts in the middle and goes across first. Some names have two capitals, such as Mary-Jane or McKay: copy them as written.

Write your child's name on a card the way school will teach it, and let them copy it, trace over it and find it on pegs, cups and drawings. In the lab your child picks Leo's and Ava's cards from look-alikes, builds Leo from big and small tiles, puts mixed-up letters back in order, traces Leo from each start dot, and writes their own name card.

practice.hint: Check every letter, not just the first one. Leo is L, e, o.
practice.explain: Leo is L, e, o. Lee ends in e, and Leon has one letter too many.

practice.prompt: Your name has {n} letters. Only the first one is a big letter. How many small letters does it have?
practice.hint: One letter is big: the first. The rest are small. Take away 1.
practice.explain: {n} letters, and 1 of them is big, so {=n-1} are small letters.

practice.prompt: Which is Ava written the right way?
practice.hint: A name starts with a big letter. What about the rest?
practice.explain: Ava starts with a big A, a capital. The rest, v and a, are small letters.

practice.prompt: Your name card has {n} letters. You have written {k} of them. How many letters are left to write?
practice.hint: Look at the card and count the letters you have not written yet.
practice.explain: {n} letters take away the {k} you wrote leaves {=n-k} more to write.

practice.prompt: Where do you start writing your name?
practice.hint: Which way do we read a line of words?
practice.explain: We write from left to right, so the first letter goes on the left.

pool.prompt: e, L, o has all of Leo's letters. Does it say Leo?
choices: Yes, all the letters are there
Yes, because it has a big L
pool.hint: Do the letters go in the same order as on Leo's card?
pool.explain: No. A name says the name only when its letters go in order: L, e, o.

pool.prompt: How does Leo start his name?
pool.hint: The first letter of a name is a capital.
pool.explain: Leo starts with a big L, a capital. Then come small e and small o.

pool.prompt: Where does the letter o start?
pool.hint: Round letters like o, a and c all start in the same place.
pool.explain: o starts at the top and goes round, the way of a c, back to the top.

pool.hint: Look at each letter: A, then v, then a.
pool.explain: Ava is A, v, a. Ada has a d in the middle, and Eva starts with E.

pool.prompt: Ben writes his name {n} times. How many big B letters does he write?
pool.hint: Each time he writes Ben, only the first letter is big.
pool.explain: One big B each time, so {n} names make {n} big B letters.

pool.prompt: Mia writes MIA. What should she fix?
choices: Make i and a small letters
pool.hint: Only the first letter of a name is big.
pool.explain: Only M stays big. The rest are small letters: Mia.

pool.prompt: Mia writes a big M, then {k} small letters. How many letters has she written in all?
pool.hint: Count the big M as 1, then count on the small letters.
pool.explain: 1 big M and {k} small letters make {=k+1} letters. Only the first one is big.

pool.prompt: Lee starts with L, like Leo. Is it Leo's card?
pool.hint: Look at the last letter of each name.
pool.explain: No. Lee ends in e and Leo ends in o. Check every letter, not just the first one.

pool.prompt: Where does the letter e start?
pool.hint: e goes across first, then round.
pool.explain: e starts in the middle, goes across, then up and round.
